Summary A preliminary assessment by researchers from Nanyang Technological University and the Singapore University of Social Sciences estimates that Singapore's 2026 haze episode cost its economy approximately S$2.32 billion, surpassing the inflation-adjusted cost of the 2015 crisis.
 The increased costs are attributed to factors such as population growth, rising incomes, and a greater health burden despite fewer hazy days.
 Researchers Quah and Or advocate for funding prevention measures and propose a "victim-pays" approach, where affected countries finance alternatives to land clearing by burning to reduce future haze risks.
 They caution against equating economic losses with equivalent prevention budgets, suggesting phased funding with measurable outcomes.

 Subscribe SINGAPORE, Nov 8 — Singapore’s 2026 haze episode has cost its economy an estimated S$2.32 billion (RM7.34 billion), exceeding the inflation-adjusted cost of the 2015 crisis despite fewer hazy days and lower average pollution levels, according to a preliminary assessment by two university researchers.
 The estimated losses as at October 31 were about 4 per cent higher than the inflation-adjusted S$2.23 billion estimated for 2015, Singapore’s The Business Times reported.
 The assessment, by Nanyang Technological University’s Euston Quah and Singapore University of Social Sciences’ Eugene Or, attributed the higher cost to population growth, rising incomes, increased visitor spending and a greater estimated health burden.
 Health-related costs, including medical treatment and the economic impact of illness and premature deaths, were higher than in 2015, as were tourism losses.
 However, losses from time taken off work and other activities due to illness, along with spending on protective measures such as masks, declined because of the shorter and less severe haze episode.
 The assessment also factored in the impact on public well-being, including people’s willingness to pay for cleaner air.
 “The sheer scale of this damage strengthens the case for funding prevention alongside tougher penalties,” the researchers said.
 Quah and Or suggested that Singapore and other affected countries could help finance alternatives to land clearing by burning, particularly in Indonesia, to reduce the risk of future haze episodes.
 Under a proposed “victim-pays” approach, countries affected by haze would contribute towards making fire-free practices more affordable.
 “If supporting fire-free practices costs less than the damage avoided, contributing can leave these countries better off,” they said.
 The researchers acknowledged that the proposal raised questions of fairness, stressing that companies responsible for fires should still be held accountable.
 They also cautioned against treating the estimated economic losses as justification for equivalent spending on prevention.
 “A S$2.32 billion haze bill does not automatically justify a S$2.32 billion prevention budget,” they said, calling for phased funding tied to measurable results.
 They added that any proposed intervention would also require a thorough cost-benefit analysis to ensure public money was directed towards measures that meaningfully reduced fire risks.
